Creators who need a clean version of an episode currently have several options:

record episode → identify explicit language → censor it manually or with an existing editing/censoring tool → review the result → export

Some creators handle this manually in their editor. Others use professional editing software with censoring capabilities, a dedicated profanity-censoring tool, or outsource the work.

The common friction is not necessarily the absence of censoring technology — it is adding another editing task, tool, or workflow to podcast production.

The problem is not simply that profanity exists.

The pain is the production work required to create a clean version when the creator decides one is needed.

For creators concerned with sponsors, advertisers, broader distribution, or simply having multiple versions of an episode available, this can become repetitive work on every release.

Manually censoring explicit language is slow and repetitive.
Every occurrence has to be found, edited, timed correctly, and checked. On conversational content, this can mean repeating the same mechanical task throughout a long recording.

Create a clean version without turning censoring into a separate production workflow.
The advantage is not that automatic censoring exists nowhere else. The advantage is that it is built into the same environment where the creator can edit the transcript, clean the voice, remove fillers and silences, add chapters and music, and export the finished episode.

Censoring should be part of podcast editing — not another job after it.

The emotional contrast is:
“Another production step” → “Already handled inside Cast.”

What if podcast censoring was automatic?
